question: In what year did World War I end?
notes: Fact: the armistice took effect on 11 November 1918. 1919 left out of the wrong answers since the Treaty of Versailles was signed then.

question: In 1914, British and German soldiers along parts of the Western Front stopped fighting, swapped gifts and sang carols in an unofficial truce named after which holiday?
notes: Fact: the Christmas Truce of December 1914, unofficial and patchy along the line.

question: Which German fighter ace was nicknamed the Red Baron?
notes: Fact: the top-scoring ace of the war, known for his red-painted planes; killed in April 1918.

question: Which armored fighting vehicle, given a code name to keep it secret, first went into battle with the British army in 1916?
notes: Fact: first used at Flers-Courcelette (part of the Somme), 15 Sept 1916; 'tank' was a cover name suggesting water tanks.

question: What were German submarines commonly called in World War I?
notes: Fact: from the German Unterseeboot. Q-ships were British decoys; E-boats were WWII German motor torpedo boats.

question: Which U.S. president led the country into World War I?
notes: Fact: Wilson asked Congress to declare war on Germany in April 1917.

question: Which flower, which bloomed on the battlefields of Flanders, became the symbol of remembrance for those who died in World War I?
notes: Fact: inspired by John McCrae's poem 'In Flanders Fields'. Cornflower (France) and forget-me-not (Newfoundland) left out as wrong answers.

question: Who was Germany's emperor, or Kaiser, during World War I?
notes: Fact: Kaiser Wilhelm II reigned 1888-1918 and abdicated in November 1918.

question: In which year did Britain and France declare war on Germany?
notes: Fact: both declared war on 3 September 1939, two days after Germany invaded Poland.

question: Which U.S. naval base in Hawaii did Japan attack by surprise on December 7, 1941?
notes: Fact: the attack on Pearl Harbor, Oahu, Hawaii, brought the U.S. into the war. Guam and Wake were hit the same day but are not in Hawaii; Dutch Harbor (Alaska) was attacked in June 1942.

question: On D-Day, June 6, 1944, Allied troops stormed the beaches of which region of France?
notes: Fact: the landings were on the Normandy coast. Provence was invaded in August 1944 (Operation Dragoon); Pas-de-Calais was the decoy target.

question: Which U.S. president led America into World War II but died in office weeks before Germany surrendered?
notes: Fact: FDR died 12 April 1945; Germany surrendered 7-8 May 1945. Truman succeeded him.

question: Which Fascist dictator led Italy into World War II as Germany's ally?
notes: Fact: Mussolini declared war on Britain and France on 10 June 1940. Franco kept Spain out of the war; Badoglio replaced Mussolini in 1943.

question: Who led the Soviet Union throughout World War II?
notes: Fact: Stalin led the USSR from the late 1920s until his death in 1953. Lenin died in 1924; Khrushchev led from 1953.

question: What name is given to the 1940 air campaign in which the RAF fought off the German air force over southern England?
notes: Fact: July-October 1940. The Battle of Berlin and the Battle of the Ruhr were later RAF bombing campaigns over Germany (1943-44).

question: What name was given to Japanese pilots who deliberately crashed their planes into Allied ships?
notes: Fact: kamikaze ("divine wind") attacks began in October 1944 at Leyte Gulf.

question: Which American general was Supreme Allied Commander for D-Day and later became U.S. president?
notes: Fact: Eisenhower was Supreme Commander, Allied Expeditionary Force; U.S. president 1953-1961. None of the others became president.

question: In which year did World War II end?
notes: Fact: Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan in August-September 1945.

question: What nickname, from a wartime song, came to stand for American women working in defense factories?
notes: Fact: the song "Rosie the Riveter" (Redd Evans and John Jacob Loeb) was a 1943 hit; Norman Rockwell's Rosie cover followed. "Sweet Rosie O'Grady" is an 1896 song.

question: What does the "E" stand for in VE Day, celebrated on May 8?
notes: Fact: VE Day = Victory in Europe Day, 8 May 1945 (9 May in the USSR).

question: Which young Bosnian Serb shot and killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914?
notes: Fact: Princip fired the shots in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. Wrong answers are other assassins of the era (none in the Sarajevo plot); the Franz Ferdinand question in world_history asks the victim, not the assassin.

question: Austria-Hungary's declaration of war on which country, in July 1914, began World War I?
notes: Fact: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914.

question: Germany's invasion of which neutral country in August 1914 brought Britain into the war?
notes: Fact: Britain had guaranteed Belgian neutrality (1839 Treaty of London). Luxembourg left out: Germany occupied it too.

question: Which British ocean liner was sunk by a German submarine off the coast of Ireland in May 1915, helping turn American opinion against Germany?
notes: Fact: torpedoed by U-20 on 7 May 1915. Liners sunk by U-boats or their mines (Britannic, Arabic, Carpathia, Laconia) left out of the wrong answers.

question: Which huge British and French offensive, beginning on July 1, 1916, was named after a river in northern France?
notes: Fact: the Somme offensive ran July-November 1916.

question: In which year did the United States enter World War I?
notes: Fact: Congress declared war on Germany on 6 April 1917.

question: Which international organization, set up after World War I to keep the peace, was the forerunner of the United Nations?
notes: Fact: created by the peace treaties of 1919, first met in 1920, replaced by the UN in 1945-46.

question: Which giant German airships, named after the count who developed them, carried out bombing raids on Britain?
notes: Fact: Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin; raids on Britain began in January 1915. Schutte-Lanz airships (which also raided) left out.

question: The U.S. Marine Corps' famous "code talkers" in the Pacific sent messages in which Native American language?
notes: Fact: the Marine Corps recruited Navajo code talkers from 1942; their code was never broken. Code talkers from other nations (e.g., Comanche, Hopi, Meskwaki) served mostly in the Army, so those are left out of the wrong answers.

question: Which American general vowed "I shall return" when he was ordered to leave the Philippines in 1942?
notes: Fact: MacArthur said it in Australia in March 1942 and returned at Leyte in October 1944. Wainwright stayed behind and was captured.

question: Which elliptical-winged fighter, designed by R.J. Mitchell, became the RAF's most famous plane of the war?
notes: Fact: Mitchell (Supermarine) designed the Spitfire, first flown 1936. The Hurricane was Sydney Camm's design (Hawker) with straight-tapered wings.

question: Which German word, meaning "lightning war," names fast attacks led by tanks and dive bombers?
notes: Fact: Blitz = lightning, Krieg = war. Lebensraum = living space, Anschluss = union (annexation of Austria), Panzerfaust = an anti-tank weapon.

question: What was the code name for Germany's June 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union?
notes: Fact: launched 22 June 1941, named for Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. Citadel = Kursk 1943; Case Yellow = invasion of France and the Low Countries 1940.

question: What popular name was given to Germany's surprise offensive through the Ardennes forest in December 1944?
wrong_1: The Battle of the Hürtgen Forest
wrong_4: The Battle of the Falaise Pocket
notes: Fact: began 16 December 1944; named for the bulge it pushed into the Allied line. Hürtgen Forest (Sept-Dec 1944) and Aachen (Oct 1944) were Allied attacks just north.

question: Which German field marshal was nicknamed "the Desert Fox"?
notes: Fact: Rommel earned the nickname commanding the Afrika Korps in North Africa, 1941-43.

question: Joe Rosenthal's famous photo shows U.S. Marines raising the flag on Mount Suribachi, on which island?
notes: Fact: "Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima," 23 February 1945; it won the Pulitzer Prize.

question: Which Japanese emperor announced his country's surrender in a radio broadcast in August of the war's final year?
notes: Fact: Hirohito (Emperor Shōwa) broadcast the surrender on 15 August 1945. Akihito was his son; Taishō his father; Meiji his grandfather.

question: Which French general led the Free French from London after France fell in 1940?
notes: Fact: de Gaulle's Appeal of 18 June 1940 was broadcast by the BBC from London. Pétain led Vichy France; Foch was a WWI marshal (died 1929).

question: Which British prime minister came home from Munich in 1938 promising "peace for our time"?
notes: Fact: Chamberlain, 30 September 1938, after the Munich Agreement. Often misquoted as "peace in our time."

question: Under which 1941 U.S. program were weapons and supplies sent to Britain, the Soviet Union and other Allies?
notes: Fact: the Lend-Lease Act was signed in March 1941. Cash and Carry (1939) and Destroyers for Bases (1940) came before it; the Marshall Plan (1948) after.

question: Which secret German message, decoded by British intelligence, offered Mexico an alliance against the United States?
notes: Fact: sent January 1917 by Foreign Secretary Arthur Zimmermann, decoded by the Admiralty's Room 40, published in the US in March 1917.

question: Australian and New Zealand troops landed in April 1915 on which peninsula, a landing remembered every year on Anzac Day?
notes: Fact: the Gallipoli landings of 25 April 1915, in the Ottoman Empire (today Turkey).

question: T. E. Lawrence, "Lawrence of Arabia," helped lead an Arab revolt against which empire?
notes: Fact: the Arab Revolt of 1916-1918 against Ottoman rule.

question: Which 1914 battle stopped the German advance on Paris, with French reinforcements famously rushed to the front in Paris taxis?
answer: The First Battle of the Marne
notes: Fact: September 1914; the 'taxis of the Marne' carried troops from Paris.

question: Which British war minister's stern face and pointing finger appeared on the famous 1914 "Wants You" recruiting poster?
notes: Fact: Alfred Leete's 'Britons: Lord Kitchener Wants You' (1914). Lloyd George became war minister only in 1916.

question: Which British soldier-poet wrote "Dulce et Decorum Est" and was killed just a week before the fighting ended?
notes: Fact: Owen was killed on 4 November 1918; the armistice was 11 November.

question: The U.S. president's wartime plan for peace, calling for open diplomacy, freedom of the seas and lower trade barriers, is known by what name?
notes: Fact: Wilson's speech to Congress of 8 January 1918; points 1-3 are open covenants, freedom of the seas, removal of economic barriers.

question: What was Germany's pre-war plan to defeat France quickly by sweeping around its fortified border, before turning to fight Russia?
notes: Fact: drawn up by Alfred von Schlieffen, modified by Moltke. Plan XVII was France's plan; Operation Michael was Germany's 1918 spring offensive.

question: What was the code name for the November 1942 Allied landings in French North Africa?
notes: Fact: Torch landed in Morocco and Algeria on 8 November 1942. Husky = Sicily, Avalanche = Salerno, Shingle = Anzio, Dragoon = southern France, Jubilee = Dieppe, Compass = Libya/Egypt 1940.

question: Operation Husky, in July 1943, was the Allied invasion of which island?
notes: Fact: the invasion of Sicily began 10 July 1943.

question: Which September 1944 airborne operation tried to seize a chain of Dutch bridges, ending in defeat at Arnhem?
notes: Fact: Market Garden, 17-25 September 1944 ("A Bridge Too Far"). Varsity and Plunder were the March 1945 Rhine crossings.

question: Which 1942 battle in Egypt, won by Montgomery's Eighth Army, turned the tide of the desert war?
notes: Fact: Second Battle of El Alamein, October-November 1942. Alam el Halfa (also Montgomery, Egypt, 1942) is left out of the wrong answers as arguable.

question: Which American general, known for his ivory-handled revolvers, led the Third Army across France in 1944?
notes: Fact: Patton's Third Army became operational in France on 1 August 1944. Hodges led the First Army; Clark the Fifth in Italy.

question: Which admiral, commander of Japan's Combined Fleet, conceived the December 1941 surprise attack on Hawaii?
notes: Fact: Yamamoto commanded the Combined Fleet 1939-43 and planned Pearl Harbor. Nagumo (strike commander) and Genda (detailed planner) are left out as arguable. Koga succeeded Yamamoto.

question: Which German battleship, after sinking HMS Hood, was hunted down and sunk by the Royal Navy in May 1941?
notes: Fact: Hood sank 24 May 1941; Bismarck was sunk 27 May 1941. Prinz Eugen sailed with Bismarck but escaped.

question: Juno Beach, one of the five D-Day landing beaches, was assigned to troops from which country?
notes: Fact: the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division landed at Juno. Gold and Sword were British; Utah and Omaha American.

question: Codebreakers from which country first cracked the German Enigma machine, then shared their secrets with Britain and France just before the war?
notes: Fact: Marian Rejewski and the Polish Cipher Bureau broke Enigma in 1932-33 and briefed the British and French at Pyry in July 1939. French intelligence supplied documents but did not break it.

question: At which Black Sea resort did the "Big Three" Allied leaders meet in February of the war's final year to plan the postwar world?
notes: Fact: the Yalta Conference, 4-11 February 1945, in Crimea. Tehran was 1943; Potsdam July-August 1945.

question: Which German officer planted the briefcase bomb in the failed July 1944 plot to kill Hitler?
notes: Fact: Stauffenberg left the bomb at the Wolf's Lair on 20 July 1944. Schlabrendorff planted a bomb on Hitler's plane in 1943 (it failed to go off).

question: On the deck of which U.S. battleship did Japan formally sign its surrender in Tokyo Bay on September 2?
notes: Fact: the surrender was signed aboard USS Missouri on 2 September 1945.

question: In August 1914, German forces destroyed an invading Russian army at which battle in East Prussia?
notes: Fact: 26-30 August 1914, Hindenburg and Ludendorff defeated Samsonov's Second Army. Masurian Lakes (Sept 1914) and Gumbinnen left out.

question: Austro-German forces broke the Italian lines and sent Italy's army into retreat at which battle, later described in Hemingway's "A Farewell to Arms"?
notes: Fact: October-November 1917, also called the Twelfth Battle of the Isonzo (so Isonzo is left out of the wrong answers).

question: In which battle did all four Canadian divisions attack together for the first time, a victory that became a symbol of Canadian nationhood?
notes: Fact: 9-12 April 1917, part of the wider Battle of Arras (so Arras is left out of the wrong answers).

question: In which forest was the armistice ending the fighting of World War I signed, in a railway carriage, in November?
notes: Fact: signed in Marshal Foch's railway carriage at Compiègne on 11 November 1918.

question: The 1916 Russian offensive against Austria-Hungary, one of Russia's greatest successes of the war, is named after which general?
notes: Fact: the Brusilov Offensive, June-September 1916.

question: Which American songwriter wrote the rousing World War I song "Over There," with its promise that "the Yanks are coming"?
notes: Fact: Cohan wrote it in April 1917, just after the US declared war.

question: Which treaty, signed with Germany and its allies, took Bolshevik Russia out of the war?
notes: Fact: signed 3 March 1918.

question: In April 1915, Germany made the first large-scale poison gas attack on the Western Front, releasing it from cylinders. Which gas was it?
notes: Fact: 22 April 1915 at the Second Battle of Ypres. Mustard gas came in 1917; phosgene was added later in 1915.

question: Which Bletchley Park machine, built by Tommy Flowers to attack the Lorenz cipher, is often called the first programmable electronic digital computer?
notes: Fact: Colossus Mark 1 worked from early 1944. The Bombe was electromechanical (for Enigma); Z3 electromechanical; ENIAC 1945; Manchester Baby 1948.

question: What was the name of Britain's network of coastal radar stations that gave early warning of German air raids?
notes: Fact: Chain Home, built from 1937 on Watson-Watt's work. The Kammhuber Line was Germany's radar-guided night-fighter belt; GHQ Line a British anti-invasion defence line.

question: What was the code name for the mass evacuation of children from British cities at the very start of the war?
notes: Fact: Operation Pied Piper began 1 September 1939. Aerial and Cycle evacuated troops from France in 1940; Fish shipped Britain's gold to Canada.

question: What was the code name for the deception, with a phantom army and dummy tanks, that convinced Germany the main D-Day landing would come at Calais?
notes: Fact: Fortitude South (part of the wider Plan Bodyguard, left out of the wrong answers as arguable) used the fictional FUSAG. Mincemeat was the 1943 Sicily deception; Neptune the naval assault.

question: Fought off the Philippines in October 1944, which is often called the largest naval battle in history?
wrong_1: The Battle of the Philippine Sea
wrong_2: The Battle of the Coral Sea
wrong_3: The Battle of the Java Sea
wrong_5: The Battle of the Santa Cruz Islands
notes: Fact: Leyte Gulf, 23-26 October 1944. The Philippine Sea (June 1944) was fought near the Marianas. Surigao Strait is part of Leyte Gulf, so it is left out.

question: What was the code name for the huge Soviet offensive of summer 1944 that destroyed Germany's Army Group Centre?
notes: Fact: Bagration began 22 June 1944 in Belarus. Uranus = Stalingrad encirclement 1942; Iskra = Leningrad 1943; Kutuzov = Orel 1943; Citadel was German (Kursk).

question: What name was given to the prefabricated harbours towed across the Channel to supply the Allies after D-Day?
notes: Fact: two Mulberry harbours (A at Omaha, B at Arromanches). PLUTO was a fuel pipeline; Habbakuk a proposed ice aircraft carrier. Gooseberry, Phoenix and Whale (parts of Mulberry) are left out.

question: Which Swedish diplomat saved thousands of Jews in Budapest by issuing protective passports?
notes: Fact: Wallenberg issued Schutz-Pässe in Budapest in 1944. Bernadotte (Swedish) led the 1945 White Buses rescue, not in Budapest; Sugihara (Japanese, Lithuania) and Sousa Mendes (Portuguese, Bordeaux) issued visas.

question: Which Soviet foreign minister gave his name both to a pact with Nazi Germany and to a homemade firebomb?
notes: Fact: the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact (August 1939); Finns named the Molotov cocktail during the Winter War. Litvinov was his predecessor.

question: Which British engineer designed the "bouncing bomb" used in the 1943 Dambusters raid?
notes: Fact: Wallis designed Upkeep; Guy Gibson led 617 Squadron on the raid (May 1943). Whittle = jet engine, Watson-Watt = radar, Camm = Hurricane.

question: Which Australian city was bombed by Japanese aircraft in February 1942, the first attack on the Australian mainland?
notes: Fact: 19 February 1942. Sydney was attacked by midget submarines and shelled in mid-1942, but not bombed from the air.

question: Which July 1943 clash in Russia is often called the largest tank battle in history?
notes: Fact: Kursk began 5 July 1943 (German Operation Citadel). Prokhorovka was part of it, so it is left out; some historians give the title to Brody (1941), also left out.
